query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the formation and persistence of a stable protective oxide layer during exposure above 900 °C is governed by the selective oxidation of the X-element. When X = Al, the alloy forms a slow-growing, coherent, and adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale that effectively retards further oxidation. In contrast, alloys with X = Mn or Si form less coherent, more rapidly growing oxides that are prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys produced as single- or multiphase metallic solid solutions with controlled compositions and similar microstructures, differing only in the choice of X (Al, Mn, or Si).
generation.intervention: Replace the reactive element X with Al instead of Mn or Si in otherwise identical CrFeCoNiX alloys, then expose them to high-temperature oxidative or corrosive environments.
generation.conditions: Samples are exposed in a controlled furnace at temperatures above 900 °C (e.g., around 950 °C) in a dry air atmosphere for extended durations (e.g., 100–200 hours). In some experiments, additional thermal cycling may be applied to assess scale adhesion under mechanical strain from temperature fluctuations.
generation.structural_mediator: The nature of the oxide scale—specifically, the formation of a continuous and adherent Al2O3 layer versus discontinuous or mismatched oxide scales from Mn or Si.
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation drives the formation of a desirable alumina scale when Al is present: Al oxidizes to form a thermodynamically stable, low-growth-rate oxide with a good match in thermal expansion relative to the alloy. In contrast, Mn or Si oxidizes to form oxides that grow more rapidly, are less adherent, and develop internal stresses that lead to cracking and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with X = Al will exhibit a coherent, persistent, and protective alumina scale during prolonged high-temperature exposure, whereas alloys with X = Mn or Si will show unstable oxide layers marked by cracks and spallation that compromise the protective barrier.
generation.baseline: CrFeCoNiX alloys where X = Mn or Si serve as the baseline, with the expectation that they form less protective oxide scales compared to the Al-containing alloy.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys in a single- or multiphase solid-solution state exposed to oxidative or corrosive atmospheres at temperatures above 900 °C. It assumes comparable processing routes and microstructures; deviations in secondary phase formation or extreme compositional variations may yield different oxidation behaviors.
generation.uncertainty: Precise quantification of differences in oxide growth kinetics and the threshold for scale spallation are not defined here and will require systematic experimentation across different alloy compositions and exposure conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate three sets of CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Al, Mn, or Si using an identical casting and thermomechanical processing route. Subject the samples to exposure at 950 °C in a dry air atmosphere for 100–200 hours, followed by controlled thermal cycling to simulate service conditions. Characterize the oxide scale on each sample using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to assess continuity, phase composition, and adhesion.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (via SEM/TEM)
Phase identification of the oxide (via XRD)
Adhesion and spallation tendency through thermal cycling tests
Crack density and scale integrity (microscopy analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloy does not develop a continuous, adherent alumina scale or exhibits oxide cracking and spallation comparable to the Mn- or Si-containing alloys, then the hypothesis that selective oxidation of Al produces superior oxidation protection is falsified.
